codex.title: Your Codex
codex.subtitle: {n} of {of} ideas found
codex.empty: Ideas you meet in play appear here, each with your own numbers.
why.codex.title: Your Codex
why.codex.how: A card is found the first time you meet its idea in play, after you've seen what happened, with your own numbers.
why.codex.hidden: Cards you haven't met yet stay hidden. Open the Codex from the Menu to read the ones you've found.
why.codex.lesson: You learn an idea best right after it happened to you.
codex.diminishingReturns.title: Diminishing returns
codex.diminishingReturns.text: Each extra unit of an input adds less than the one before, and past a point it adds nothing. A field already near its best gains little from more fertiliser.
codex.diminishingReturns.numbers: On a field you gave chemical fertiliser, everything together came to {n0} the usual yield, but no field gives more than {n1}: the last of the fertiliser bought nothing.
codex.diminishingReturns.world: Farmers who doubled their urea over the decades got far less than double the wheat: the soil and the plant set a ceiling.
codex.soilFertility.title: Soil fertility
codex.soilFertility.text: Fertility is the soil's store of food for plants. Every crop draws on it; lentils, a fallow season and compost put it back. Run it down and every later crop yields less.
codex.soilFertility.numbers: A harvest left one of your acres at fertility {n0} of 100. That crop uses about {n1} a season; compost puts back more than a crop takes.
codex.soilFertility.world: Indian farmers rotate wheat or rice with pulses and spread farmyard manure to keep their soil from running down.
codex.opportunityCost.title: Opportunity cost
codex.opportunityCost.text: The opportunity cost of a choice is the best thing you gave up to make it. An hour spent one way can't be spent another.
codex.opportunityCost.numbers: You earned {n0} at day labour while {n1} of your own acres stood empty.
codex.opportunityCost.world: A farmer who works for wages in town at sowing time earns cash now, but may lose a season's crop on his own land.
codex.profitNotCash.title: Profit is not cash
codex.profitNotCash.text: Profit is what a season earned less what it cost. Cash is the money in hand. Money can leave without being a cost (a loan repaid, a gift, seed bought ahead) and arrive without being income (a loan taken).
codex.profitNotCash.numbers: A season ended with a profit of {n0}, yet your cash changed by {n1}.
codex.profitNotCash.world: A shop can show a profit and still run out of money to pay its supplier. That's why businesses keep a profit and loss statement and a cash flow statement.
codex.interest.title: Interest and compounding
codex.interest.text: Interest is the price of borrowing: a share of what you owe, each season. Left unpaid, interest joins the debt and earns interest itself: that is compounding.
codex.interest.numbers: Last season your loans cost {n0} in interest, on {n1} still owed.
codex.interest.world: At 6% a season, a debt left unpaid doubles in about three years; at a bank's 2.5% a season, in about seven.
codex.creditScore.title: Credit score
codex.creditScore.text: A credit score sums up how you've handled debt: paying on time raises it, missing a payment lowers it. Lenders lend more, and cheaper, to a higher score.
codex.creditScore.numbers: Your credit score went from {n0} to {n1}.
codex.creditScore.world: In India, credit scores such as CIBIL's run from 300 to 900, and banks look at them before every loan.
codex.leverage.title: Leverage
codex.leverage.text: Leverage is using borrowed money to do more than your own money allows. It multiplies a good season's gain, and a bad season's loss.
codex.leverage.numbers: You borrowed {n0}, more than your last season's farm profit of {n1}.
codex.leverage.world: A tractor bought on a loan pays if it earns more than its instalments; in a drought year the instalments still come.
codex.liquidity.title: Liquidity
codex.liquidity.text: Liquidity is how quickly what you own can become cash. Land and buildings are worth a lot but take time to sell; a bill wants cash today.
codex.liquidity.numbers: You had {n0} in cash when a payment was refused, though you owned {n1} in land, buildings, stock and more.
codex.liquidity.world: Many farmers are land-rich and cash-poor: they borrow at sowing time though they own acres worth lakhs.
codex.inflation.title: Inflation
codex.inflation.text: Inflation is prices rising over time. The same coins buy less: seed, wages and land cost more, and what you sell fetches more too.
codex.inflation.numbers: Prices in the region are now {n0} above where your farm started.
codex.inflation.world: Prices in India have risen by around 5% a year on average: what cost 100 rupees in 2010 cost about 200 by 2024.
codex.workingCapital.title: Working capital
codex.workingCapital.text: Working capital is the money a business needs between paying for its inputs and wages and being paid for what it sells. With too little, it borrows to keep going.
codex.workingCapital.numbers: Your business is using {n0} of its overdraft, which goes up to {n1}.
codex.workingCapital.world: A kirana shop buys stock on credit from its wholesaler and pays once customers have bought it: that credit is its working capital.
codex.grossMargin.title: Gross margin
codex.grossMargin.text: Gross margin is what's left of sales after the cost of the goods sold, before wages, rent and other costs. It has to pay for everything else.
codex.grossMargin.numbers: Your business sold {n0} last season, and the goods it sold cost {n1}: a gross margin of {n2}.
codex.grossMargin.world: A halwai's milk and sugar cost about half a sweet's price; the other half pays the cook, the shop and his profit.
codex.fixedVariable.title: Fixed and variable costs
codex.fixedVariable.text: Variable costs rise and fall with what you sell, like ingredients. Fixed costs stay the same whatever you sell, like a wage or a rent. When sales fall, fixed costs don't.
codex.fixedVariable.numbers: Your business's sales fell from {n0} to {n1}, but its wage and rent still came to {n2}.
codex.fixedVariable.world: A tea stall pays its pitch rent in a slow week just as in a busy one; only the milk it buys goes down with the customers.
codex.breakEven.title: Break-even
codex.breakEven.text: A business breaks even when its sales just cover all its costs. Below that it loses money; above it, every extra sale adds profit.
codex.breakEven.numbers: Your business's plan expected {n0} of sales a season against {n1} of costs.
codex.breakEven.world: Before a bank lends to a new shop, it asks how many customers a day the shop needs to break even, and whether the street has them.
codex.forecastActual.title: Forecast and actual
codex.forecastActual.text: A forecast is your best guess before you start. Comparing it with what happened shows which guesses were wrong, so the next plan is better.
codex.forecastActual.numbers: Your business's plan expected a profit of {n0} a season; it has made {n1} a season on average.
codex.forecastActual.world: Companies compare their budget with their actual results every quarter; the gaps teach them more than the forecast did.
codex.unitEconomics.title: Unit economics
codex.unitEconomics.text: Unit economics is the profit or loss on one unit: what one kilo or one item costs to make against what it sells for. If one unit loses money, selling more loses more.
codex.unitEconomics.numbers: A kilo of what your business makes costs {n0} to make and sells for about {n1}.
codex.unitEconomics.world: A chaiwala knows to the paisa what a cup's milk, tea and sugar cost: that's what tells him his price.
codex.depreciation.title: Depreciation
codex.depreciation.text: Depreciation is the cost of an asset wearing out, spread over its useful life. No cash moves, but the asset is worth a little less each season.
codex.depreciation.numbers: Last season your buildings and machines wore down by {n0}; they're now on your books at {n1}.
codex.depreciation.world: A tractor bought for 6 lakh may be worth half that after seven or eight years of work.
codex.appreciation.title: Appreciation
codex.appreciation.text: Appreciation is an asset growing in value, like land as prices rise and the village grows. It only becomes money when you sell.
codex.appreciation.numbers: Land you paid {n0} for is now worth {n1}.
codex.appreciation.world: Farmland near growing towns in India has often risen in price faster than prices in general.
codex.yield.title: Yield
codex.yield.text: Yield is the income an asset pays each season or year, as a share of what it cost. It lets you compare a house, a deposit or a shop.
codex.yield.numbers: A family paid you {n0} in rent this season: {n1} of what their house cost you.
codex.yield.world: A house in an Indian city often yields 2–4% a year in rent, while a bank deposit pays 6–7%.
codex.hiringUncertainty.title: Hiring under uncertainty
codex.hiringUncertainty.text: When you hire, you can't see how good someone will be; you guess from what you can learn. A reference check costs a little and narrows the guess.
codex.hiringUncertainty.numbers: You paid {n0} to check an applicant's reference before deciding.
codex.hiringUncertainty.world: Employers call a candidate's last employer because a bad hire costs far more than the call.
codex.marketWage.title: The market wage
codex.marketWage.text: The market wage is what workers can earn elsewhere. Offer less and the good ones go to whoever pays it.
codex.marketWage.numbers: You offered {n0}; the applicant asked for {n1} instead.
codex.marketWage.world: When building work booms in a district, farm wages there rise too: labourers can earn more on the sites.
codex.retention.title: Retention
codex.retention.text: Retention is keeping the people you have. Replacing a skilled worker costs more than a fair raise: the search, the training and the work lost meanwhile.
codex.retention.numbers: Your worker is paid {n0} a season; another employer offered {n1}.
codex.retention.world: Businesses often find it cheaper to match an offer than to hire and train someone new.
codex.trainingRoi.title: Return on training
codex.trainingRoi.text: Return on investment compares what something cost with what it brings back. A course costs money and days away; a more skilled worker gives more for years.
codex.trainingRoi.numbers: A course raised your worker's skill to {n0}.
codex.trainingRoi.world: Governments pay for skills training because a trained worker earns and produces more for the rest of their working life.
codex.employerReputation.title: Employer reputation
codex.employerReputation.text: Your reputation as an employer is what workers hear about you: fair pay, paid on time, help when it's needed. Good workers come to a good name, and stay.
codex.employerReputation.numbers: Your name as an employer now stands at {n0}.
codex.employerReputation.world: In a village everyone knows who pays on time; a bad name empties the queue at your gate.
codex.publicGoods.title: Public goods
codex.publicGoods.text: A public good is one everyone can use, and one person's use doesn't take from another's: a school, a road, a clean pond. Nobody can sell it for a profit, so it's built when someone gives it or the government does.
codex.publicGoods.numbers: The school you gave cost {n0}. Children at it now, free: {n1}.
codex.publicGoods.world: Most of India's village schools, roads and wells were built by the government or by donors, not by markets.
codex.longTermInvestment.title: Long-term investment
codex.longTermInvestment.text: A long-term investment pays back slowly, over years, not seasons. A child who can read will earn more all their life.
codex.longTermInvestment.numbers: A child finished {n0} years at your school and can read; the school cost you {n1}.
codex.longTermInvestment.world: Studies across India find each extra year of schooling raises a person's earnings by around 5–10%.
codex.publicMoney.title: Public money
codex.publicMoney.text: A town spends other people's money: grants and taxes, not its own earnings. It keeps its own books, apart from any one person's, and it may only spend what it has.
codex.publicMoney.numbers: The district gave your town {n0} to start. It is the town's, not yours.
codex.publicMoney.world: A village panchayat keeps a separate account for grants and taxes, audited apart from its members' own money.
codex.budgetPriority.title: A budget is a priority list

hub.why.trendChange: Over these seasons: {coins} in today's coins; {counted} as counted then; prices rose {prices}.
hub.why.trendText: Net worth counted at each close, restated in today's coins by the price index of that close, so a rise is a real rise, not only prices.
hub.why.made: What your wealth is made of
hub.why.madeText: Each share is of everything you own, before what you owe. A pie that is mostly land is wealth you can't spend; cash is what pays the bills.
hub.why.debtOwe: What you owe: loans and interest due
hub.why.debtText: What you owe divided by what you own, rounded down. Under {comfortable} is comfortable, over {risky} is risky: one bad season could cost you land.
hub.why.emergencyText: Cash and savings divided by what the next season close takes, rounded down. Your family's living counts at the basic plan at least. Under one season is amber.
hub.why.passiveRent: Rent from your houses, land and godown
hub.why.passiveBusiness: Profit of businesses run by a hired worker
hub.why.passiveText: Last season's income that came without your own labour, against your family's living. A business that lost money counts against it. The farm isn't counted: you still decide and sow.

notify.TreasuryShort.body: Open the game before the season ends: a gift, a tax or the budget can cover it.
why.away.Savings: The co-op bank added the season's interest to your deposit, and where it says your savings paid the close, a yes from you (or your standing choice) covered what your cash couldn't.
ledger.savingsCover: Your savings paid the close, with your yes
hub.why.savingsText: Put in and take out any time. The interest is added to the deposit at every close, before the statements, so it earns interest too. It counts in your emergency fund and in passive income, never as collateral, and no lender can take it.
hub.why.pricesDeposit: What the deposit earns a season
hub.why.pricesText: Prices rise a little every season. Cash in hand loses that much value. A deposit earns more than prices usually rise, so the savings keep up.
hub.why.standing: If cash runs short at the close
hub.why.standingText: Ask me: on the last day of the season you're warned, and nothing leaves your savings unless you say yes. Always pay from my savings: the bank pays what's short from your savings at the close, up to what you hold, and the season report says so.

milestone.firstLakh.done: Your cash and savings, less what you owe, reached a lakh.
milestone.firstLakh.todo: Cash and savings, less what you owe: {have} of {target}.
milestone.firstLakh.why: Your cash plus your savings deposit, less every loan and its interest, counted at a season's close. Borrowed cash is cash, but you owe it, so it doesn't count. The target is {target}: a lakh, whatever prices do.
milestone.twiceInherited.done: Your net worth reached twice the estate you started with, in today's coins.
milestone.twiceInherited.todo: Net worth {have} of {target}: {times} times your {inherited} inheritance, in today's coins.
milestone.twiceInherited.why: Your net worth at a close against {times} times what you inherited. The inheritance is counted in the coins of that close, so prices rising doesn't make it easier.
milestone.firstRent.done: A family paid you rent for the first time.
milestone.firstRent.todo: A family living on your land pays you rent.
milestone.firstRent.why: Reached at the first close where a family on your land had paid you rent.
milestone.debtFree.todo: Repay your last loan. A write-off at a foreclosure doesn't count.
milestone.debtFree.why: Reached when none of your own loans is open and the last one closed by being repaid. A foreclosure's write-off doesn't count, and a business's loan is on its own books.
milestone.passiveCoversLiving.done: Rent, interest and your hired businesses paid your family's living.
milestone.passiveCoversLiving.todo: Rent, interest and hired businesses cover {pct}% of your family's living.
milestone.passiveCoversLiving.why: Reached at a close where rent, interest on your savings and the profit of businesses you've hired out paid at least {pct}% of your family's living.

why.treasury.balance.text: A fund balance isn't profit. It is what the town can spend. Public money lives in its own books and never mixes with yours.

why.treasury.rents.text: The rent your shops pay for the square's pitches is the town's money. It is counted only when a rent is really paid.
why.treasury.gifts.title: Gifts from you
why.treasury.gifts.text: A gift goes one way. The town never pays you back.

why.treasury.dept.office: The clerk collects what the town is owed. At full pay the office collects all of it; a clerk paid less collects less.
why.treasury.dept.health: Health pays the clinic's doctor and its upkeep.
why.treasury.dept.education: The district pays the teacher. The town keeps the school open.
why.treasury.dept.roads: Roads pays for the link road and the lanes.
why.treasury.dept.safety: Safety pays the watchman, the community hall and the playground.
why.treasury.dept.utilities: Utilities pays for water and power.
why.treasury.dept.policies: Policies pays what your enacted policies cost.

why.tax.house.title: House tax
why.tax.house.text: You own the houses, so you pay the tax on them: that is what raising it costs you. Your own home counts as a kutcha house and a hand's hut pays nothing. The council's office collects its share of the bill, and you pay only what it collects.

why.tax.business.text: Your businesses pay from their own cash on a season's profit; a loss pays nothing. The village's shops keep no books, so they pay on a reference profit.
why.tax.collected.title: Collected last season
why.tax.collected.text: The council's office collects what is billed. A clerk paid less collects less, and the payer pays only what is collected.

policy.tourTitle: Policies: a trade, never a gift
policy.tour: A policy helps some people and costs others. The town pays for it from the town's money, never yours, though some also cost you. You can have three at a time. Each starts a season or two after you enact it, and you can repeal it. You don't need any: a town left alone runs fine.
policy.leftAlone: A town left alone runs fine with no policy. Enact one only when you want the trade.

policy.meals.name: Free school meals
policy.meals.helps: poorer families' food and children's health
policy.meals.how: A fixed sum for each pupil, for the pupils the school has now: {n}
policy.meals.why: Every child at the school eats a meal there, paid by the town, so their families need about a quarter less food at home. Hungry families get closer to eating enough, and children's health rises a little each season. The food is bought from the district's supplier, never from your store, stall or businesses.
policy.meals.afterRepeal: Families buy all of their children's food again.
policy.subsidy.name: Farm input subsidy
policy.subsidy.helps: your neighbours' farms and the town's food prices
policy.subsidy.costs: the town's money, and you: crops sell a little cheaper
policy.subsidy.how: A fixed sum for each acre your neighbours farm: {n} acres
policy.subsidy.why: The town pays part of your neighbours' seed and fertiliser. They grow a little more, and local crop prices fall by about a coin in a hundred or two. That helps families' food budgets, and it costs you a little on what you sell at the local market. If you repeal it, prices dip for two seasons before they settle.
policy.subsidy.afterRepeal: Crop prices dip a little for two seasons, then settle.
policy.grant.name: Small business grant
policy.grant.helps: a family with no work, and shoppers
policy.grant.costs: the town's money, and your shops: a new competitor
policy.grant.how: A fixed sum, one grant a season
policy.grant.why: Each season the town offers a grant to help someone open a small shop. About four in ten come to nothing: the money is spent and no shop opens. The rest let a newcomer open in a trade the village needs. A new shop pays business tax, and it competes with yours.
policy.grant.afterRepeal: No more grants. Shops already opened stay open.
policy.minWage.name: Minimum wage
policy.minWage.helps: your hands, your businesses' workers and labourers from your town
policy.minWage.costs: you and your businesses: wages rise 10% above the market
policy.minWage.how: An inspector's pay, a fixed sum
policy.minWage.why: No wage may be less than 10% above the market wage: a hand's season, a labourer's day, a business worker's pay and the town clerk's. Wages you already pay rise at each contract's next renewal; a new ask is higher at once. The town's own clerk is paid the minimum too, which costs the town a little more than the inspector. Fewer newcomers open shops, because wages cost them more.
policy.minWage.afterRepeal: Wages stay where they are until each contract renews.
policy.rentControl.name: Rent control
policy.rentControl.helps: tenants: a renewal rises by at most 3% a year
policy.rentControl.costs: you, as a landlord: your rents fall behind prices
policy.rentControl.how: A rent officer's pay, a fixed sum
policy.rentControl.why: When a lease renews, its rent may rise by at most 3% instead of 10%. A new family moving into an empty house still pays the market rent, and no rent goes down. Fewer families leave over rent, but your rent income grows more slowly.
policy.rentControl.afterRepeal: Renewals move back toward the market, by at most 10%.

why.clinic.share.title: The community share
why.clinic.share.base: A clinic's share in year-0 coins
why.clinic.share.text: The district builds the clinic, but a village is asked for its share: about 40% of what it costs. You pay it once, as a gift to the village. It is not an investment, never part of your farm's profit, and you don't get it back. It follows the price index like every coin amount.
why.clinic.lesson: A community share is how a village shares the cost of public works with the district, as real panchayats do.
why.clinic.days.title: Time to build
why.clinic.days.text: The district's builders take two days. The clinic opens when they are done.
why.clinic.quarters.title: The doctor's quarters
why.clinic.quarters.text: A doctor will not come without a house. The quarters are a larger house on the plot beside the dairy. They stay yours: an asset that earns the doctor's rent once he lives there.
why.clinic.arrives.title: When the doctor comes
why.clinic.arrives.text: A doctor from another village arrives a day after both the clinic and the quarters stand, and moves in with his family.
why.clinic.doctor.title: The doctor
why.clinic.doctor.text: A clinic with no doctor covers nobody. While he is in post the clinic works for every home in its reach. He and his family count as one of your households.
why.clinic.doctor.left: He left because his allowance went unpaid. A new doctor comes at the first close when the Health service is back to {pct} and the town has his allowance.
why.clinic.pays.title: Who pays the doctor
why.clinic.pays.district: Until the Township the district pays his salary, his allowance and the clinic's upkeep. You owe nothing recurring.
why.clinic.pays.budget: From the Township your town's Health budget pays his allowance and the clinic's upkeep each season. Money never comes from you, and the town never pays you.
why.clinic.service.title: The Health service
why.clinic.service.leave: The doctor leaves if it stays under
why.clinic.service.text: How well the Health department is funded. Each close it moves halfway to what it was paid. It scales every effect of the clinic. If it stays under the line for two closes, the doctor leaves.
why.clinic.reach.title: The clinic's reach
why.clinic.reach.text: A home is covered if it is no farther than this from the clinic, counted in whole acres of 100 m between two tiles. Out of reach, a home gets nothing and its sheet says so. Today every home on the map is inside it.
why.clinic.capacity.title: The clinic's capacity
why.clinic.capacity.text: The clinic serves this many people at full strength. With more, every effect shrinks slowly in proportion: never a cliff.
why.clinic.avoided.title: Sick days avoided
why.clinic.avoided.text: Each day you, your hands and your workers might fall ill; the game draws one number for that day. With the clinic the chance is cut by {pct} (at full service). A day counts here only when the same number would have made someone ill without the clinic. It is an exact count, not a guess.
why.clinic.regained.title: People whose health stands higher
why.clinic.regained.text: At each close a person's health falls if food was short and rises if they were fed. With the clinic it falls less and rises faster. This counts the people whose health ended higher than it would have without it.
why.clinic.elders.title: Elders who stayed well
why.clinic.elders.text: Each close an elder faces a chance of passing away. With the clinic it is cut by {pct} (at full service). This counts the elders who would have died by that same draw without the clinic and did not.
why.clinic.e.sick.title: Fewer sick days
why.clinic.e.sick.text: The chance that you, a hand or a worker falls ill on a day is cut by this much. The effect is the full cut times the Health service times the capacity share.
why.clinic.e.loss.title: Less health lost to hunger
why.clinic.e.loss.text: When a family cannot eat enough, health falls each season. The clinic cuts that loss by this much.
why.clinic.e.gain.title: Faster recovery
why.clinic.e.gain.text: A fed person recovers a little health each season. The clinic makes that recovery faster by this much.
why.clinic.e.death.title: Elders live longer
why.clinic.e.death.text: The chance that an elder passes away in a season is cut by this much: about three more years of life on average.
why.clinic.e.care.title: The Health care need
why.clinic.e.care.text: A household's health care need is half met by the chemist. The clinic meets the other half, scaled by its effect, which lifts the household's security and so its happiness.
why.clinic.status.title: The village clinic
why.clinic.status.text: The district builds a clinic for the village once it is a village, for the share you give. It works only with a doctor.
why.quarters.cost.title: What the quarters cost
why.quarters.cost.base: A larger house in year-0 coins
why.quarters.cost.text: You pay the builders and keep the house: it is an asset at cost, like any house of yours, and it loses a little value each season. You may borrow toward it.
why.quarters.days.title: Time to build
why.quarters.rent.title: The doctor's rent
why.quarters.rent.text: The doctor pays this each close from his salary, like a family in one of your houses: about the same yield on the cost as a 60,000 house at 2,500 a season. If he leaves, the quarters wait for the next doctor and you lose the rent till then.
why.quarters.book.title: Book value
why.quarters.book.text: What the quarters cost, less the depreciation so far: a little each season over their life.
why.quarters.household.title: The doctor's household
why.quarters.household.text: One to three people. They count as one of your households and are literate, so they count toward the Township's literacy goal.

progress.subtitle.township: What your village needs to become a Township
progress.townshipOrder: The usual order: homes and the road first, then the clinic. The doctor needs his house, and the old village comes with the Township.
progress.open.taxes: House and business taxes, and five policies
progress.open.cohort: The old village joins you: about {n} families, {people} people
letter.township:
Beta, a village feeds itself; a township looks after itself. Fifteen families make their homes on your land, the clinic has its doctor, the road to the highway is paved, three trades have paid their way and most of the village can read. It is a Township now.

The district has opened the town's treasury with a start-up grant, and the old village has joined us: about thirty families, a hundred and fifty people, who will look to the council the way they once looked to your grandfather. Taxes, a budget and policies are yours to decide for everyone's sake. Remember the one rule of public money: it is the town's, not yours, and it never pays you. And if you leave it all alone, nothing breaks.
cohort.tax: House tax they paid last close
why.township.lesson: A Township is earned by looking after people: homes, a doctor, a road, work and reading.
why.township.households.title: Households of yours
why.township.households.text: Families living on your land: in your family houses, in your huts, and the doctor's household in his quarters.
why.township.households.next: Next: build family houses on your acres and let families move in.
why.township.clinic.title: The village clinic
why.township.clinic.text: The clinic must be built and have a doctor in post. A doctor comes a day after the clinic and his quarters both stand.
why.township.clinic.next: Next: pay the community share at the clinic plot, then build the doctor's quarters on the plot beside the dairy.
why.township.road.title: The paved link road
why.township.road.text: A paved road to the highway brings you better prices for what the trader buys.
why.township.road.next: Next: petition for it at the council hall once you have 10 households.
why.township.businesses.title: Businesses with a profitable season
why.township.businesses.text: Three open businesses must be open, each with at least one season that made a profit on its own books. A closed business does not count, hired or run by you.
why.township.businesses.next: Next: found a business and run it through a profitable season.
why.township.literacy.title: Literacy
why.township.literacy.text: The share of your households' people aged 7 and over who can read must reach the goal. Children learn at the school; adults learn in its evening class.
why.township.literacy.next: Next: start an adult class at the school, and let the children go.
why.cohort.happiness.title: The old village's happiness
why.cohort.security: Security: work, health care and rent
why.cohort.belonging: Belonging: the temple and the banyan square
why.cohort.growth: Growth: the school and their leisure
why.cohort.happiness.text: The same four layers as a household's, each from what the town really gives them: they eat from their own income, the clinic reaches them when it has a doctor, the school takes their unlettered children free, and the house tax comes out of their leisure and savings. Under {below} for {closes} closes in a row, one household leaves. A town left alone keeps them.
why.cohort.pupils.title: Children at your school
why.cohort.pupils.text: About one in fifteen of the old village's people is a school-age child who cannot read yet. They join your school free; a second teacher comes when pupils pass 30.
why.cohort.literacy.title: Who can read
why.cohort.literacy.text: Of the old village's people aged 7 and over. It is for the statistics: the Township's literacy goal counts only your households.
why.cohort.tax.title: The house tax they paid
why.cohort.tax.text: The old village pays the house tax like you do, from its own budget: first from leisure, then from savings, never from food. The office collects its share and the treasury is paid what they pay.
why.cohort.village.title: The old village
why.cohort.village.text: The families who lived here before you. They are one record, not people with cards: they count as residents for the grants, send their children to your school and pay house tax.
why.netWorth.taxOwed: House tax you owe the town
stmt.bs.taxOwed.why: House tax carried from a close you could not pay. It is paid first at the next close, and it counts against your net worth.

why.minWage.above: While the minimum wage is in force no ask or renewal can be below it. This wage is above it, so the floor changes nothing today.
why.minWage.binds: While the minimum wage is in force no ask or renewal can be below it, so this wage is raised to it.
why.civic.cost.title: What it costs
why.civic.cost.text: The town pays a builder from its own cash. It is kept as the town's asset and wears out a little each season. Your cash isn't touched.
why.civic.upkeep.title: The upkeep
why.civic.upkeep.text: Each close the Safety budget pays this to keep the building in repair, whether or not anyone is in it.
why.civic.wage.title: The wage
why.civic.wage.text: A fixed scale from the town's content, moved with prices, with no negotiation. It is paid from Safety before the upkeep, and it is the old village's income. The minimum wage, if enacted, would not change it: the scale is already above it.
why.civic.who.title: Who keeps it
why.civic.who.text: The post is not hired from the board. You advertise it and a villager of the old village takes it within a day; his name is on the sheet.
why.civic.who.none: A playground needs no one to keep it.
why.civic.keeper.title: The post
why.civic.keeper.text: A post with nobody in it covers nobody. If his wage goes unpaid in full at {leave} closes running, he leaves and the post covers nobody until you post it again. After you post it, a villager takes it in {hours} hours.
why.civic.pays.title: Who pays
why.civic.pays.text: The Safety department pays these each close, after the departments before it. Unpaid, the service wears down, half the gap each season.
why.civic.service.title: The Safety service
why.civic.service.text: The Safety department's funding, moving halfway to what it is paid each close. The building's benefit is multiplied by it.
why.civic.reach.title: The reach
why.civic.reach.text: A home is covered if its distance (metres between two tiles, an acre is 100 m) is within the reach. Homes out of reach get nothing, and their sheet says so.
why.civic.capacity.title: The capacity
why.civic.capacity.text: If more people than its capacity are served, the benefit is scaled down by capacity ÷ people: a slow decline, never a cliff.
why.civic.watchman.effect.title: Safety for homes in reach
why.civic.watchman.effect.text: Safety is a fourth part of a home's security once a post stands: 50% with nobody in it, up to 100% with a watchman in reach. It is added to the job, health care and rent, so security moves a little, never more than a quarter of the gap.
why.civic.hall.effect.title: Belonging for homes in reach
why.civic.hall.effect.text: The temple and the square give 80%. With a caretaker in the hall the home's Belonging rises towards 100%, times the Safety service and the share the hall can serve.
why.civic.playground.effect.title: Play for homes with children
why.civic.playground.effect.text: A home with children has leisure of 30% when it has money for it. A playground in reach adds up to 30% more, times the Safety service and the share it can serve. Homes without children get nothing.
why.civic.cash.title: The town's cash
why.civic.cash.text: The town's cash, not yours. It is paid for the building at once. Grants, taxes, rents and your gifts fill it.
why.civic.status.title: The plot
why.civic.status.text: The town's money opens with the Township; the plot waits until then.

why.landValue.water: Clean water near (the pond or a well within {m} m, or a working water tower)
why.landValue.read: It is read once a season, at the close, so it never jumps while you are looking. Rent, price and tax all follow it.
why.landValue.lesson: What is near an acre makes it worth more: a road, water, the school and clinic, the square, jobs and neighbours. A growing town lifts every acre in it, yours too.

confirm.ListParcel.title: Sell slowly?
confirm.ListParcel.warn: The acre is locked until it sells. You can take it off the market any time before. The price is fixed now.
confirm.CancelSale.title: Take it off the market?
confirm.CancelSale.warn: You can list it again, or sell it quickly, whenever you like.
confirm.BuyParcel.warnTownship: Selling it quickly fetches {quick} of its price; selling slowly, over 2 days, fetches all of it.
reject.AlreadyZoned: That land is zoned so already.
away.builderYours: A builder bought your land for {price} and built homes on it.
away.builderTheirs: Builders bought a neighbour's land by the road and built homes on it.
confirm.ZoneParcel.title: Offer to builders?
confirm.ZoneParcel.warn: The land leaves yours when it sells, and homes are built on it. Nothing happens until families are waiting. You can take it back to farming before then.
zone.housesNote: Builders may buy this land when families are waiting
zone.hint: A builder buys at most one parcel a season. If you sow it, builders skip it until it is empty again.
builders.familiesNote: Residents of the town: grants, shops and happiness count them. Not your households.
household.rentBuilder: {rent} a season, paid to the builder
why.waiting.title: Families waiting for a home
why.waiting.so: Families that found no home so far
why.waiting.each: Each acre of a parcel needs
why.waiting.no: not yet: a builder needs both
why.waiting.fee: The town gets a permit fee of
why.waiting.feeTown: {pct} of the price of the land
why.waiting.text: Families come to the valley and look for a home. When they find none they are remembered, and when enough are waiting a builder buys land that has a road and water near it.
why.waiting.lesson: Zoning only says you are willing to sell. Builders build where families wait and the land is worth it.
lease.startNote: {rent} a season, paid at each close
lease.activeNote: Rent comes at each close, upfront
lease.hint: While it is leased you can't sow, build, zone or sell it. The soil stays as it is.
lease.cant.use: Empty the acre first: a crop, a tree or a building is on it.
lease.cant.order: Take the hand's order off this acre first.
lease.cant.water: A pump, borewell, channel or drip is on this acre, so it can't be leased.
lease.cant.zoned: Take it back to farming first.
lands.leased: Leased · rent {rent} a season · next close in {left}
lands.leaseStarting: Leased from the next close · rent {rent} a season
lands.leaseEnding: Lease ends at the close in {left}
confirm.LeaseOutLand.title: Lease this land out?
confirm.LeaseOutLand.warn: You keep the land. A neighbour farms it and the soil stays as it is. While it is leased you can't sow, build, zone or sell it. You can end the lease; it ends at a close.
confirm.EndLease.title: End the lease?
confirm.EndLease.warn: Nothing is refunded and nothing is owed. From the close you can sow, build, zone or sell it again.
confirm.EndLease.afterValue: no more rent; the land is yours to use
reject.Leased: That land is leased out. End the lease first; it ends at a close.
event.LandRentPaid: Rent came in for your land.
away.leaseEnded: The lease on your {what} ended. It is yours to use again.
ledger.landLeased: Rent from a neighbour for your leased land
why.landRent.title: The rent a season
why.landRent.worth: What the land is worth today
why.landRent.soilValue: stays as it was: a tenant neither wears it out nor builds it up
why.landRent.text: A tenant farms the land and pays you rent. If the town makes your land worth more, the rent rises with it at the next close.
why.landRent.lesson: Land earns even when you don't work it. Rent is a safe, small return on what the land is worth. Farming it yourself, or with a hand, can earn more, and takes work and risk.
cash.row.4210.out: Rent from your leased land, given back
needs.schoolFar: The school is {m} m away; its reach is {reach} m
road.upkeepTreasury: The town's treasury, in its Roads line
season.LandRentReceived.why: A neighbour farms your leased land and pays a season's rent when it begins, whatever the harvest.
place.generator_plot.line: A diesel generator can stand here at the town's edge: it lights the village's shops in the evening, and its smoke lowers the land near it.
place.spare_plot.line: Kept free for a later public building.
place.tower_plot.line: The town can build a water tower here, so homes beyond the wells have water.
place.drains_plot.line: The town can lay drains from here, for health and for the land's value.
place.collection_plot.line: The town can keep a collector's post here, so the lanes stay clean.
place.grid_plot.line: The district's power line meets the town here, once the town pays its share.
place.village_well.line: A well the old families dug, beside their lane. Builders look for water within 300 m of it.
place.tea_stall_well: The highway tea stall and its well
place.tea_stall_well.line: Lorry drivers stop here for chai. Its well gives the road's south side water.
place.old_house.line: One of the old village's families lives here, part of the town's records, not a person with a card.
village.river.line: The valley's river. It runs along the north and bends south at the corner. Never for sale.
village.scrub.line: Wild land at the edge of the valley. Never for sale.
lane.does: The two acres of this section become a road, so the acres beside them can be reached by cart.
lane.guardFine: Your own cash isn't touched. With today's income the town can still pay its bills at the next close.
lane.guardShort: Your own cash isn't touched. With today's income the town would be short by {amount} at the next close.
why.lane.cost.title: Cost of a lane section
why.lane.cost.text: Two acres of gravel laid by a village builder, paid by the town. Prices follow the district's, so a section costs more as everything does. It lasts about 80 seasons, and the town writes off a little of it at each close.
why.lane.progress.title: Sections built on this lane
why.lane.progress.text: A lane is built a section at a time, and nothing has to be built first, so the town can build as it can afford it. A road acre lifts the land value, the rent and the builders' interest in the acres beside it.
build.civicSub: The town is building it from its own money.
build.title: Building materials
build.subtitle: The trader's stock for today; it fills again at its hour.
build.notYet: Buildings take materials and masons from the Township.
build.cardGang: The gang: {days} days at one and a half times
build.timingNow: Its materials are in today and the masons start now: ready in about {time}.
build.timingHeld: The trader's stock for the whole town can't cover the {good} it needs today, so it waits for more: ready in about {time}.
build.moneyYours: Your money is in the building from today.
build.moneyTown: The town's money is in the building from today.
board.masonsNone: No mason in town yet: the district's gang builds, at one and a half times.
board.masonsNote: A mason is a grown-up of your town with no town job and a craftsman's hands. A build pays a mason for each day he works, into his household. When none is free, the district's gang builds at one and a half times.
why.civic.cost.masons: The masons' days, at their own price
why.civic.cost.gang: The district's gang: the masons' days at one and a half times
why.civic.cost.textBuilt: The town pays a builder from its own cash, in full when it starts: bricks, cement and timber at the trader's prices and the masons' days. It is kept as the town's asset and wears out a little each season. Your cash isn't touched.
why.build.stock.title: What the trader still sells today
why.build.stock.limit: The trader's limit a day, for the whole town
why.build.stock.text: The trader sells only this much to the whole town in a day, and it fills again at {hour}:00. Your builds and the town's draw first, in the order they began; the builders' homes draw after.
why.build.masonsTown.title: Masons in town
why.build.masonsTown.text: A mason is a grown-up of your town with no town job and a craftsman's hands. A build keeps the free ones from its start and pays each {day} for every day he works, into his household.
why.build.builders.title: Builders' homes waiting
why.build.builders.text: The builders' homes take the same materials, after yours and the town's, so a brick shortage slows them first.
why.build.gone.title: Finished
why.build.good.title: {good} for this building
why.build.good.limit: The trader sells a day, for the whole town
why.build.good.text: It takes the {good} a little at a time from the trader's day, after any build that began before it, and the building starts when all its materials are in.
why.build.masons.title: Who builds it
why.build.masons.pay: Masons' pay, paid when you started
why.build.masons.text: The masons kept for it work its days at {day} a day, paid into their households when it is finished. More masons build it in fewer hours.
why.build.masons.gang: No mason was free when it began, so the district's gang builds it: one and a half times the price of the masons' days (a day is {day}) and one and a half times the hours.
why.build.ready.title: When it will be ready
why.build.ready.hours: Hours of building once its materials are in
why.build.ready.text: The days its materials take from the trader's daily limit, then its hours divided by its masons.
why.build.status.title: Where it stands
why.build.status.text: A building is paid for in full when it starts. It then waits when the trader's stock for the day is used up, and the masons build it once its materials are in.
village.lane: A track for a gravel lane
village.lane.line: The town can build a gravel lane here, so the acres beside it have a road. Never for sale.
village.laneBuilt.line: The town built this lane, so the acres beside it have a road. Never for sale.
village.highway.line: The district's highway along the valley's south edge. Never for sale.
closed.ring.line: This land opens when the village becomes a Township.
closed.hills.line: These hills open with the Township, for apple orchards.
utility.tower.title: Water tower
utility.tower.plotSub: A plot in the village · the district builds it from the town's cash
utility.tower.whoValue: No one: it works by itself
utility.tower.effect: Homes past the pond and wells
utility.tower.effectNote: Without clean water near, builders skip the land and the people there lose health every season.
utility.tower.lineOn: Working: it waters the homes in its reach.
utility.tower.cardSub: On the village plot · the town pays
utility.generator.title: Diesel generator
utility.generator.plotSub: A plot on the edge of the map · the district fits it from the town's cash
utility.generator.whoValue: No one: it runs by itself
utility.generator.effectWill: lamps and fans, and evenings at the usual wage
utility.generator.effectNote: Its smoke lowers land value and health around it. The grid has no smoke, no fuel and no limit of people.
utility.generator.lineOn: Working: power for the homes and shops in its reach.
utility.generator.cardSub: On the edge plot · the town pays
utility.grid.title: Grid connection
utility.grid.plotSub: On the highway side · the district's line, the town's share
utility.grid.whoValue: The district's line: nobody to keep
utility.grid.effectWill: lamps and fans, evenings at the usual wage, and no smoke
utility.grid.effectNote: A generator that stands is switched off, and its upkeep, fuel and smoke stop.
utility.grid.lineOn: Working: power for the whole town.
utility.grid.cardSub: On the highway side · the town pays
utility.drains.title: Drains
utility.drains.plotSub: A plot in the village · the district builds them from the town's cash
utility.drains.whoValue: No one: they work by themselves
utility.drains.effectWill: keep their health and their land's value
utility.drains.effectOn: keep their health and their land's value
utility.drains.effectNote: Without drains, once the town is big enough to need them, Health service is held down, people lose health and acres with homes lose land value.
utility.drains.lineOn: Working: it drains the homes in its reach.
utility.drains.cardSub: On the village plot · the town pays
utility.collection.title: Collection post
utility.collection.plotSub: A plot in the village · the district builds it from the town's cash
utility.collection.whoValue: A collector, hired by the town like the clerk
utility.collection.extra: The collector's wage a season, from Utilities
utility.collection.effectNote: Without it, once the town is big enough to need it, every household's Belonging is lower.
utility.collection.lineOn: Working: a collector keeps the town clean.
utility.collection.cardSub: On the village plot · the town pays
utility.lockedNote: The town's money opens with the Township; the plot waits until then.
utility.smokeIs: land value {lv} points lower on {acres}; health {health} points lower a season in {homes}
utility.poorNote: The town is {short} short. Give it some, then build.
utility.lineUnpaid: Not working: the town has not paid its upkeep.
utility.offNote: The grid replaced it. Its upkeep and fuel stopped, and so did its smoke.
utility.serviceStopped: Under {pct} it covers nobody until the town pays its upkeep again.
utility.tower.only: Homes it waters that the pond and wells don't
utility.power.shopsValue: evenings at the usual wage ({n} hours)
utility.gridNote: The grid costs {extra} more and saves {saves} a season: about {n} seasons to come back. It has no smoke and no limit of people.
utility.guardAdds: It adds {amount} a season to Utilities.
utility.guardGrid: The generator is switched off and its upkeep stops: you save {saves} a season and its smoke goes. The extra {extra} comes back in about {n} seasons.
utility.guardShort: At today's income the town would be short by {amount} a season: raise a tax or save elsewhere.
utility.guardFine: The town can pay it from what it takes in.
utility.guardSmoke: Its smoke lowers land value on {acres} and the health of {homes}.
utility.costs: What the four cost the town a season
away.gridConnected: The grid is connected: the generator is switched off.
why.utility.cost.title: What the {name} costs
why.utility.cost.fitted: The district fits it the same day, with no bricks or masons: the price is its base price moved by today's prices.
why.utility.upkeep.title: The upkeep
why.utility.upkeep.text: Each close the Utilities budget pays this to keep it running, whether or not anyone needs it that season.
why.utility.generator.extra.title: The fuel
why.utility.generator.extra.text: Diesel for the lamps and fans of up to 300 people a season, at today's prices. The grid needs none.
why.utility.collection.extra.title: The collector's wage
why.utility.collection.extra.text: The town hires the collector as it hires its clerk. His wage is paid at the close, first in the department, and is the old village's income.
why.utility.reach.title: The reach
why.utility.reach.text: A home is covered if its acre is within {m} metres of the plot (an acre is 100 m, counted along the roads). Homes out of reach get nothing, and their sheet says so.
why.utility.reach.whole: The district's line and the collector's round cover the whole town.
why.utility.capacity.title: The capacity
why.utility.capacity.text: If more people than its capacity live in town, each home is served a little less: its share of the capacity, a slow decline and never a cliff.
why.utility.capacity.none: The grid has no limit of people.
why.utility.service.title: The service
why.utility.service.text: The Utilities department's condition: each close it moves halfway toward how much of its budget was paid. Under the floor it covers nobody.
why.utility.floor: The floor, under which it covers nobody
why.utility.homes.title: Homes it waters
why.utility.homes.text: Homes of your households with no pond or well within 300 metres but a working tower within its reach.
why.utility.who.title: Who keeps it
why.utility.who.none: Nobody tends it: the district's builders fit it and the Utilities budget pays its upkeep.
why.utility.who.collector: The collector is hired and paid by the town like the clerk: no post to advertise, and his wage is the old village's income.
why.utility.evening.title: Evenings at the usual wage
why.utility.evening.text: A shop or workshop within reach of power can open that many hours past its usual close without the long day's extra pay.
why.utility.tower.effect.title: Clean water
why.utility.tower.health: Health a home beyond water loses a season, in points
why.utility.tower.effect.text: Homes within 300 metres of the pond or a well, or within the tower's reach, have clean water. Past it, builders skip the land and people lose a fifth of what a season short of food costs them, every season.
why.utility.generator.effect.title: Power
why.utility.grid.effect.title: Power
why.utility.generator.effect.text: Homes in reach have lamps and fans: their Leisure need is a tenth higher. Shops and workshops in reach keep evening hours at the usual wage.
why.utility.grid.effect.text: The same as the generator, for the whole town, with no smoke and no limit of people.
why.utility.drains.effect.title: Drains
why.utility.drains.health: Health a home beyond the drains loses a season, in points
why.utility.drains.cap: What Health's service can reach without them
why.utility.drains.land: Land value an acre with a home loses, in points
why.utility.townSize: Residents from which the town needs it
why.utility.drains.effect.text: Once the town has that many residents, homes beyond working drains lose health, the Health service is held down, and acres with a home standing lose land value. Drains in reach stop all three.
why.utility.collection.effect.title: A clean town
why.utility.collection.belonging: Belonging a household loses without it, in points
why.utility.collection.effect.text: Once the town has that many residents, a household with no working collection feels the town is dirty and its Belonging need is lower.
why.utility.smoke.title: The generator's smoke
why.utility.smoke.lv: Land value each acre loses, in points
why.utility.smoke.health: Health a home there loses a season, in points
why.utility.smoke.cap: The most land value smoke takes from one acre in all, in points
why.utility.smoke.healthCap: The most health smoke takes from one home in all, in per cent
why.utility.smoke.text: The smoke reaches two acres out along the roads. The generator stands on an edge plot so it falls on fields and ring land. The grid switches it off.
why.utility.ladder.0.title: Water
why.utility.ladder.0.text: The pond and wells serve homes within 300 metres. A water tower reaches 400 and serves up to 400 people.
why.utility.ladder.1.title: Power
why.utility.ladder.1.text: A diesel generator lights 300 people within 600 metres and smokes; the grid lights the whole town and replaces it.
why.utility.ladder.2.title: Sanitation
why.utility.ladder.2.text: Pits do until the town is big. Drains reach 500 metres and serve up to 300 people.
why.utility.ladder.3.title: Waste
why.utility.ladder.3.text: With no collection nobody takes the waste away. A collection post, with its collector, serves up to 400 people anywhere in town.
why.utility.noWater.title: Homes without clean water
why.utility.noWater.text: Homes of your households with no pond or well within {m} metres and no working water tower within {tower}.
why.utility.costs.title: What the utilities cost
why.utility.costs.text: What each standing utility costs the town every close: its upkeep, the generator's fuel and the collector's wage, at today's prices.
needs.waterTower: The water tower serves it, {m} m away.
needs.waterFar: People here lose {n} points of health a season. A water tower reaches {m} m from its plot.
needs.drainsFar: People here lose {n} points of health a season, and the town's Health service is held down.
needs.wasteFar: The town feels dirty: Belonging is {n} points lower.
event.HouseUpgradeStarted: A house is being made pucca.
confirm.UpgradeHouse.title: Upgrade to pucca?
upgrade.state.rent: Rent is over what they can pay
upgrade.state.locked: The acre is listed or leased out
upgrade.detail: {cost} · the rent rises at the renewal
upgrade.note: A pucca house is brick and concrete and lets for more. Nothing else about the family's life changes.
upgrade.warnEmpty: Nothing comes back in rent: the house is empty now.
upgrade.warnHand: Nothing comes back in rent: a hand's house is part of his pay.
upgrade.warnRent.one: Their rent stays {rent} until the lease ends this season, then rises to at most {most} and on towards {pucca}, never more than {pct}% of their income. It comes back in about {seasons} seasons: a slow choice.
upgrade.warnRent.other: Their rent stays {rent} until the lease ends in {n} seasons, then rises to at most {most} and on towards {pucca}, never more than {pct}% of their income. It comes back in about {seasons} seasons: a slow choice.
why.householdRent.pucca: The house is pucca, so its market rent is the pucca base rent times its place and prices. The rent climbs to it in steps, one at each renewal.
why.upgrade.title: Pucca upgrade
why.upgrade.gone.title: Pucca upgrade
why.upgrade.builders.title: Pucca homes built by builders
why.upgrade.builders.text: Builders make one of their homes pucca each season, where it is offered: the land is worth enough, clean water is near and the family can pay. Their bricks come after yours and the town's.
why.upgrade.text: The upgrade costs what a pucca house costs more than a kutcha one: bricks, cement and timber at today's trader prices and the masons' days. A pucca house is only worth building where the land is worth more (a road, a school, a clinic, the square, clean water and jobs near an acre raise it) and where a family can pay the higher rent. The cost comes back as the rent rises, so the payback is the cost divided by what the rent will rise by.
why.upgrade.isPucca: This house is pucca: it lets for the pucca rent. A tenant's rent climbs to it in steps, one at each renewal.
why.upgrade.making: The masons are at work. The family stays, and the rent moves only when the lease is renewed.
why.landValue.smoke: Smoke from {n} near it (a kiln or a diesel generator)
why.landValue.drains: A home here with no drains to carry the water away
why.upgrade.waterText: Clean water is the pond or a well within {m} m, or a working water tower within {tower} m.
why.upgrade.familyEmptyText: Nobody lives there, so there is no rent to bear.
why.upgrade.familyHandText: A hand pays no rent: the house is part of his pay, so nothing comes back in rent.
why.upgrade.familyYesText: The pucca rent {rent} is within {pct}% of the {income} they earn.
why.upgrade.familyNoText: The pucca rent {rent} is over {pct}% of the {income} they earn, which is {most}.
overlay.fertility.name: Fertility
overlay.fertility.title: Fertility (of 100)
overlay.fertility.none: Not a farm acre, so it has no fertility to show.
overlay.fertility.line: {soil} soil. Crops take fertility out; compost and rest put it back.
overlay.landValue.name: Land value
overlay.landValue.title: Land value
overlay.landValue.note: The fourth step starts at ×{edge}, where a pucca house is offered.
overlay.landValue.none: This is not land that can be built on, farmed or sold.
overlay.landValue.lineHigh: A pucca house can be offered here: it is at ×{edge} or more.
overlay.landValue.lineLow: A pucca house is offered from ×{edge}. Roads, water, the school and the square lift an acre.
overlay.coverage.name: Coverage
overlay.coverage.title: Services that reach the acre
overlay.coverage.note: School, clinic, watchman, clean water. Red hatching: smoke from a kiln or the generator.
overlay.coverage.none: This is not land that has services.
overlay.coverage.lineAll: All four services reach this acre.
overlay.coverage.smoke: Smoke reaches here: land value {lv} points lower and health {health} points lower a season.
overlay.happiness.name: Happiness
overlay.happiness.title: Happiness of the household
overlay.happiness.note: Only acres with one of your households are tinted. Dimmed: no household.
overlay.happiness.none: No household of yours lives here.
overlay.happiness.lineMany: {n} households live here: the number is their mean.
overlay.crime.name: Crime
overlay.crime.title: Crime
overlay.crime.note: No crime yet: this overlay lights up with the Town life update. Every acre of land stays grey.
why.coverage.title: Services at this acre
why.coverage.waterNo: No · no pond, well or tower near
why.coverage.how: Each service reaches the acres within its reach, counted in metres along the lanes (an acre is 100 m). A service that is not open or staffed reaches nobody.
why.coverage.lesson: Where a school, a clinic or clean water reaches, homes are worth more and their people are healthier. Smoke does the opposite.
why.acreHappiness.title: Happiness at this acre
why.acreHappiness.how: The number is the mean of the households living here. Each household's own Why? is on its sheet.
why.acreHappiness.lesson: Happy households stay, pay their rent and bring neighbours. Unhappy ones leave after a few low seasons.
store.inCold: {kg} of it is in the cold store in town
cold.title: Cold store in the mandi town
cold.subtitle: Potatoes and fruit keep far longer here than in the hut
cold.howNote: Potatoes, mangoes and guavas you harvest or buy go into your rented cold space first, then the hut. Nothing to carry and nothing to press. Sell or use them any time.
cold.rentHeading: Rented space in the cold store
cold.rentForcedNote: Your goods need {t} t, so it can't end yet. Sell or use them before the close and it ends. Until then the close takes {rent}.
cold.keeps: Keeps {cold} of every 100 kg over a season ({hut} in the hut)
cold.notKeptNote: Fresh vegetables, milk, grain and seed. Grain has the godown; the co-op chills the milk.
cold.worthNote: Sells at {start} now and {end} later. About {pct} on the money kept.
cold.worthNoneNote: Its price is best at once, so keeping it only costs rent.
season.due.coldStore.why: Rent for the cold space you booked or your goods in it need, paid upfront at the season's end. Without it the space ends and the goods go back to the hut store.
season.short.coldStore: your goods would go back to the hut store
why.cold.rent.title: Your cold-store space
why.cold.rent.rent: Rent a tonne for a season
why.cold.rent.how: Space is rented by the tonne for a season, a coin a kilo, paid upfront at the close, and again each season until you stop it. Potatoes and fruit fill it by themselves, what spoils fastest first.
why.cold.rent.lesson: Renting space is a cost you pay before you know the price you will get. Only keep what the season's price swing pays for.
why.cold.good.title: {good} keeps {n} of every 100 kg
why.cold.good.cold: In the cold store it spoils
why.cold.good.hutKeeps: A season is {days} days, so over one season the hut keeps
why.cold.good.how: Cold air slows the rot: potato to a tenth, fruit to a quarter. Goods the cold store does not keep spoil as they do at home.
why.cold.good.lesson: Slower spoilage is worth only what the better price and the rent leave: see Is it worth it?
why.cold.worth.title: {good}, {from} to {to}
why.cold.worth.noneHow: At today's prices no season pays more for {good} than it costs to keep it: the rent and the spoilage take the rise. It goes the wrong way.
why.cold.worth.how: That is about {pct} on the money held, and only if the later price comes: a slump loses it. The savings deposit pays 1.5% a season and carries no risk.
why.cold.worth.lesson: A price swing is not a profit until the rent, the spoilage and the risk are paid.
